title: A. Paññāvaddho: "You must be very cautious about thinking that you have attained exulted states of Dhamma. People can fall into that trap, and it’s…
content:
The Delusion of Claiming High Attainments

"You must be very cautious about thinking that you have attained exulted states of Dhamma. People can fall into that trap, and it’s a big danger. It’s all a lot of delusion. And if they talk about it, you can be sure that it isn’t true. Somebody who really has attained high states of Dhamma doesn’t talk about it. They know perfectly well that there is no benefit in talking about it. It doesn’t help to talk about it – what you are, you are. If you have reached a certain stage in your practice, that’s where you are – and that’s all. Talking about it to try to attract other people is just a matter of the kilesas. So be very wary of people who claim to have attained this or that state in their practice. Mostly, if they claim it, it’s false. And for yourself, it is useless to speculate whether you have attained this or that level of Dhamma. You on what you are, and that’s all. It’s enough that you still have plenty of work to do in meditation. As long as you are working to overcome the kilesas, then it does not matter where exactly you are on the path; what matters is that you are going in the right direction. When you believe that you have already achieved success in meditation, the tendency is to relax and stop trying, which becomes a big blockage to further progress. So always resist the idea that you have reached a safe plateau in your practice, and attainment which you cannot fall back from. Just keep striving hard and when you reach the final goal you will know it is certainty."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "When genuine remorse arises, it comes with wise attention and with a clear understanding of how causes give rise to effects. The transgressor…
content:
The Role of Genuine Remorse in Spiritual Progress

"When genuine remorse arises, it comes with wise attention and with a clear understanding of how causes give rise to effects. The transgressor reflects: 'Ah, those words I spoke—they came from anger and caused harm. This is the result of not guarding my mind'. This kind of honest reflection is valuable because it leads to real understanding and a sincere determination to change. Guilt, by contrast, is a toxic mental state that obstructs genuine spiritual development. It is a form of self-indulgence that keeps us trapped in past actions and prevents us from moving forward with wisdom and compassion. When we do something wrong—say, we speak harshly to someone or act in ways that cause harm—the mind tends to get caught up in an endless cycle of replaying that event, trying to remedy harm done in the past."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "In a sense, tanha functions as the proximate cause of suffering, while avijja serves as its root condition. One of the Buddha's teaching…
content:
The Buddha’s Medical Model for Healing the Mind

"In a sense, tanha functions as the proximate cause of suffering, while avijja serves as its root condition. One of the Buddha's teaching strategies was to start with what's most immediately recognizable and actionable, which in this case is craving. By beginning with the experience of craving—something we can perceive arising in our minds moment to moment—he provides a practical entry point for more profound insights. The practitioner who works to understand and release craving eventually encounters the deeper distortions of perception that sustain it, which are created by avijja's fundamental misunderstanding of reality. This teaching strategy reflects the medical model the Buddha often used: first identify the symptom (suffering), then diagnose the immediate cause (craving), trace that back to the underlying disease (ignorance), and lastly prescribe the appropriate medicine (the Noble Eightfold Path)."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: The Great Wheel of samsaric existence is turned by the collective craving of all living beings. Each moment of greed propels the wheel…
content:
The Collective Craving that Turns the Wheel of Samsara

The Great Wheel of samsaric existence is turned by the collective craving of all living beings. Each moment of greed propels the wheel of life and death around in continuous motion. If human consciousness were an ocean, greed would be like a particular wave pattern on its surface, while tanha would be like the underlying current that creates all waves. This current of tanha moves silently beneath the surface, shaping not just our worldly desires, but our entire relationship with existence. Greed can be modified or controlled through moral precepts and willpower, but tanha must be addressed by deep Dhamma practice and understanding. Addressing tanha properly requires a fundamental revision of how we understand ourselves and our relationship to greed. This is not about simply calming the waves on the surface; it's about comprehending the entire ocean of awareness.

title: A. Paññāvaddho: Whenever we get rid of kilesas, we feel an increase of freedom. The main aim of body contemplation is to get rid of…
content:
The Mind as the True Essential

Whenever we get rid of kilesas, we feel an increase of freedom. The main aim of body contemplation is to get rid of the kilesas. You should question any sensation arising through the senses. In essence, everything has to be a thing of mind; you need the mind for everything. Because of that, mind is the true essential here. Everything you work on in your wisdom practice will eventually come back to that. The investigation always leads back inside. While most senses are neutral, feeling knows sukha and dukkha, and the sukha or dukkha arising from other senses is actually feeling.

title: A. Paññāvaddho: If a person actually has an experience of Jhāna then a qualified teacher can discuss it with that person individually, but otherwise just…
content:
High States of Concentration and the Essential Nature of Wisdom

If a person actually has an experience of Jhāna then a qualified teacher can discuss it with that person individually, but otherwise just discussing it in a general way would not be appropriate because it is too high. Jhāna is a very high state which is beyond the average person to contemplate meaningfully. So it is wrong to equate states of samādhi that are normally experienced with Jhāna since there is not necessarily any connection at all. Jhāna is not essential to the development of wisdom and freedom from the kilesas. The factor that is absolutely essential all the time in meditation practice is mindfulness. Without mindfulness present one cannot call it meditation. Mindfulness is the rope which secures the mind firmly to the meditation object and as such is really the foundation of samādhi practice. Mindfulness, presence of mind, keeping ones attention in the present, here and now – this is central to training the mind. Mindfulness means keeping ones attention on the practice to the exclusion of everything else. Attention is the main thing. One should learn to be attentive, constantly increasing ones attention span until there are no gaps where the mind drifts away.

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Everything that happens to us, everything, comes from causes we ourselves have set in motion. This isn't fate or predestination; it's cause and…
content:
Personal Responsibility vs. Metaphysical Speculation

"Everything that happens to us, everything, comes from causes we ourselves have set in motion. This isn't fate or predestination; it's cause and effect, pure and simple. Each thought, each action, each choice we make is creating our future right now. But we fail to see this clearly because our minds are too clouded, too restricted. It was for this reason that the Buddha chose to teach people a gradual path that accorded with the level of their understanding. When people came to him with questions about the origin of the universe or the nature of the infinite, he simply remained silent. Why? Because answering these questions does not lead to freedom from suffering. The questioners are like the man shot with an arrow who refuses treatment until he knows what kind of wood the arrow was made from and who shot it, because he refuses to recognize that there is an urgent need to remove the arrow quickly."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: The practice of Dhamma is a method. You have to apply the method generally, but if, for instance, you’re out on a trek…
content:
Overcoming Obstacles in the Path

The practice of Dhamma is a method. You have to apply the method generally, but if, for instance, you’re out on a trek somewhere, you may know the general direction you should be going in, but then you run into a thick forest and you have to find a way around that because trying to bash straight through it is not the right way. It’s much the same with kammatthāna, you know the general direction you should be going in, but at any one time you may find obstacles in your path and you must find some way around them. So you search for a suitable method to overcome them. Obstacles for people practicing samādhi: you may work at ānāpānasati until you reach a point where you can’t seem to get any further. So you think that perhaps you’re doing the wrong practice and try Buddho instead. With Buddho you reach the same point and again don’t get any further. If you then review your practice carefully you’ll see that it’s caused by something in you. The fault is not in the method. Then you realize that you must choose one method and stick with it diligently until you break through that blockage. Or you may find that you have no enthusiasm for the practice, as though everything is tasteless. You realize this comes from kilesas, so you try to find a method to overcome it. You can try reading something inspiring to give you renewed energy and enthusiasm for meditation.

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Although science does stand as a remarkable tool for analysis, we must understand its proper scope and its limitations with clarity of mind.…
content:
The Circular Logic and Limits of the Scientific Method

"Although science does stand as a remarkable tool for analysis, we must understand its proper scope and its limitations with clarity of mind. When we examine the scientific method carefully, we see it deals exclusively with what can be measured, observed, and tested through the physical senses. Consider first the matter of scientific hypotheses. When scientists attempt to explain any phenomenon, they face the inherent limitation that there are endless possible rational explanations for what they observe. Like trying to identify an unseen object by its shadow alone, they imagine countless different objects that could cast that same shadow. This means they can never test every possible hypothesis and, therefore, can never arrive at an absolute proof of any scientific theory. This leads us to a deeper problem in scientific inquiry: how can science study its own methods when it lacks an independent standard of measurement? Because of this dilemma, when science attempts to validate scientific methodology using the same methodology, it creates a circular argument that undermines its own foundation."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: Using body contemplation, we can go quite a long way in Dhamma. It can lead one into quite good states of Dhamma. From…
content:
From Gross to Subtle: Contemplating the Mind

Using body contemplation, we can go quite a long way in Dhamma. It can lead one into quite good states of Dhamma. From there one can go on to investigate the mind and the ways of the mind, but that’s a little bit more esoteric. When one is contemplating the body: here’s the body, you can see it. You can see the inside of it, either by seeing another body that’s been pulled to bits, or by looking into your own body and seeing it with your mind. It’s gross. It’s not difficult to get hold of. When you come to the mind, however, it’s very subtle. So it’s difficult to get hold of, difficult to understand. And because of that, first of all you have to train yourself in wisdom to quite a large degree before you can really tackle the mind in the right way. When you can get to the mind in the right way, then all sorts of things are thought of which one had never thought of before.
